explanation.overall:
The single smartest thing this song does is refuse to name the feeling. The chorus says he's back in Chicago and that he feels it — and then never tells you what "it" is. Three lines, and the noun at the center is missing. The second line is the same trick in reverse: an older version of himself described as something he was *inside*, like a room or a coat, not something he was. Because the song withholds the object, you supply it. That's why a song about one specific person's Chicago works on someone who's never been there.

The music is built to swell, not to hit. In the measured 30 seconds, energy climbs in four small steps — 0.60, 0.73, 0.77, 0.86 — with no single jump bigger than 0.13, then spends nine seconds sliding back down to 0.29. There's no drop, no slam. Librosa clocks the pulse at 156 beats a minute across 80 beats, but the record is felt at about half that (roughly 78) — the backbeat lands on every other click, which is why something technically fast reads as a drift. Attacks come at about 2.4 a second, close to two per felt beat: steady, unsyncopated churn. Nothing pokes at you. The whole thing moves like a tide, so when the lift arrives it feels like it's rising out of you rather than being done to you.

And the writing is theatre. Characters don't get described, they get *announced* — a stage direction, then a line of their dialogue in quotation marks, both times a question or reassurance about time. He's not remembering a place. He's watching a play about himself, from the cheap seats, and the third line of the chorus is him waving at the stage.

moments.what_happens: The chorus's first line ends on an unspecified pronoun — he's back in Chicago and he feels it — and the word "it" is never given an antecedent anywhere in the song.
moments.why_it_hits: You can't be told what the feeling is, so you install your own. The hook works less like a statement and more like a blank the listener fills in with their own hometown, their own former self.

moments.what_happens: Energy rises in four small measured steps — 0.60 at 6.4s, then 0.73, 0.77, and 0.86 at 12.8s — with no jump larger than 0.13 between readings.
moments.why_it_hits: The lift you're braced for never arrives as a jolt, so the swell registers as internal — like a feeling building in you rather than an effect being fired at you. It's the sonic version of a memory surfacing instead of striking.

moments.what_happens: From the 0.86 peak the energy falls for nine straight seconds to 0.29 at 23.6s, and across the clip's three thirds the average brightness drops from 1916 Hz to 1668 to 1621 — the section loses its high end as it recedes.
moments.why_it_hits: It doesn't just get quieter, it gets duller and further away, like detail draining out of something you're remembering. The dimming is what makes the recording feel recalled rather than performed at you.

moments.what_happens: The second verse opens by announcing that the song has started and that you're only now catching up — the track breaks frame and refers to itself, mid-narrative.
moments.why_it_hits: It drags you inside the timeline. You stop overhearing someone's memory and become the person arriving late to it — which is exactly the position he's describing being in about his own life.

moments.what_happens: The proverb about taking the man out of the city runs three complete times at exactly six-second intervals — the same clock the chorus lines run on — then the fourth pass is cut off after "out of the-", followed by roughly four seconds of open space before the last chorus.
moments.why_it_hits: Three repetitions turn the line into a loop you can lean on; the fourth pulls it out from under you. The sentence stops at precisely the part he can't finish, and the silence that follows does the confessing.

explanation.lyric_read: Look at how the verses are wired: each long line rhymes with itself internally — a tear to cry against an eye, the middle of the night against black and white — so the line closes before it ends, and then the short line reaches outside to rhyme with the next short line. In verse one that outside chain is airtight: for / Troubadour / 24. In verse two it breaks — Caroline and fine still lock, but the line about it all being a laugh rhymes with nothing. The one moment the pattern fails is the one moment he's laughing at himself, and the writing lets that line hang unsupported. The chorus does its work through tense: it opens in the habitual present ("when," not "if" — this happens every time he goes back), drops into past tense for the older self, and returns to present for the waving. The goodbye is not a completed act; it's a thing he is still doing. And the title inverts the cliché — not the beginning of the end, but the end of beginning, with no article on "beginning," which turns it from an event into a condition you age out of. The clearest tell is the count: the second chorus trails four goodbyes, the last one only two. Instead of building to a climax the song thins out, running down its own supply, and stops.
explanation.headline: The chorus never names the feeling — "I feel it" leaves a blank you fill.

suggestions.title: Let It Happen
suggestions.why: Same withheld-noun hook — the chorus hangs on an "it" with no antecedent — and the same choice to mix the lead vocal inside the band rather than in front of it, so the line reads as a feeling instead of a statement.

suggestions.title: Chicago
suggestions.why: The ending abandons the verse structure and loops a single confessional line until it stops being a sentence and becomes a mantra — the exact move as the four-times proverb bridge here.

suggestions.title: Losing My Religion
suggestions.why: Builds its hook out of a borrowed idiom bent to a private meaning, the same trick as inverting "beginning of the end" and hammering the take-the-man-out-of-the-city saying into the emotional climax.
